title: UPDATE 1-Croatia cenbank buys euros to ease firming pressures on kuna  currency
text:
(Adds details)

ZAGREB, Dec 15 (Reuters) - The Croatian central bank said on Tuesday it had bought 130 million euros ($157.78 million) from commercial banks in an auction to relieve upward pressure on the kuna currency.

It said it had bought the euros at an average rate of 7.5360 kuna. The kuna was quoted at 7.5330 after the intervention from around 7.5130 earlier in the day.

In March, as the COVID-19 pandemic hit Croatia, the central bank intervened several times on the foreign exchange market to counter depreciation pressures on the kuna and sold more than two billion euros to the banks.

The last time the central bank intervened buying the euros from the commercial banks was in August 2019.

This year Croatia entered the European Exchange Mechanism (ERM-2), a waiting room of at least two years before adopting the euro. Zagreb hopes to meet all the macroeconomic criteria, like the budget gap or the public debt/GDP ratio, on time to join the euro zone in 2023.

As part of ERM-2, the European Central Bank (ECB) set the central rate of the kuna at 7.5345 per one euro ($1 = 0.8239 euros) (Reporting by Igor Ilic Editing by William Maclean)

title: UPDATE 1-Croatia cenbank buys 345.5 mln euros from banks in  forex intervention
text:
(Adds details, quotes)               

ZAGREB, Dec 13 (Reuters) - Croatia's central bank said on Wednesday it bought 345.5 million euros ($405.82 million) from commercial banks on the local foreign exchange market to prevent appreciation pressures on the kuna currency.               

It bought the euros at an average rate of 7.5605 kuna per euro. The kuna eased after the intervention to 7.5533 per euro at 1035 GMT, easing from around 7.53 before it.               

"There were some mild appreciation pressures on the kuna and apparently the central bank wanted to act preventively," a dealer at a major local bank said.               

Another market participant, who asked not to be named, said that the central bank might have also wanted to give a boost to its own balance sheet at the end of the year.               

This was the fifth central bank's intervention this year to counter appreciation pressures on the kuna and the biggest one in volume. In those five interventions it altogether bought 947 million euros from commercial banks.               

In October Croatia tentatively set a goal of adopting the euro within seven to eight years.

title: CEE MARKETS-Croatian assets surge to multi-year highs as economy improves
text:
* Recovering economy boosts kuna, dealers watch central bank
    * Zloty touches new 2-month high, stocks firm
    * Price moves muted as investors await U.S. payroll data
    * Romanian assets off lows but edgy due to political turmoil

    By Sandor Peto and Igor Ilic
    BUDAPEST/ZAGREB, Feb 3 (Reuters) - Croatia's kuna, buoyed by
an improving economy, set its firmest level in over 4 years
against the euro on Friday, while central European currencies
were mixed.
    The region's assets got support in recent days from the
Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank as neither of the
banks signaled tighter than expected policies.
    The kuna, which like the zloty gradually gained
ground in the past weeks, was the strongest since October 2012
at 7.436 on Friday. Dealers said the central bank may intervene
in the market any time to stem the rally.
    Croatia, which enjoys a robust tourism sector, has current
account surpluses. Inflation, near zero, has not been a worry so
far and the economy is also on an upswing.
    The Croatian economy returned to growth last year after a
weak decade. Retail sales data published on Thursday showed a 
robust 5.9 percent annual rise. 
    The equities indices of Warsaw and the much smaller
Zagreb bourse have been the region's top gainers this
year, with 6.4 percent and 8.5 percent rise, respectively. On
Friday the Zagreb index was the highest since August 2011.
    The Croatian government also opened books on Friday for
domestic bond issues, one of the lead arrangers said, to
refinance a 5.5-billion-kuna ($800-million) 10-year bond,
maturing on Feb. 8. 
    Elsewhere in the region, investors were on the sidelines,
awaiting more economic data from the United States.
    "Investors are cautious now ahead of the U.S. non-farm
payroll figures," one Budapest-based fixed income trader said.
Those figures are due at 1330 GMT.
    Hungarian and Polish bond yields rose 1-2 basis points.
    The forint was a tad weaker against the euro at
0936 GMT after data showing disappointing 3.2 percent annual
rise in retail sales in December. The zloty set a new
2-month high at 4.299.
    Romanian assets were off lows hit after a decree passed on
Tuesday triggered massive street protests against corruption
this week, which are likely to continue, and cracks in the
one-month-old government.  
    While inflation in Croatia is still hovering near zero, it
has rebounded in other countries of the region.
    Czech inflation has reached the central bank's target in
December. If the January data due on Feb. 10 are high, that may
refuel speculation that the bank could soon abandon its cap at
27 against the euro soon.
    The crown's exchange rate implied in six-month forward deals
 indicated that recent comments from the central
bank - including after Thursday's meeting - have tamed
speculation for early exit from the cap and a crown surge.
 
    The implied rate reached a 4-week low on Friday at 26.869
after the bank released its new inflation report.

title: Central Europe  Currencies  To Gain on 'Bremain' -- Brexit Market Talk
text:
0805 GMT Central European currencies would recover fully from their 0.8% to 3% losses against the euro last week if the U.K. votes to remain in the EU in Thursday's referendum, says Erste Bank. The Polish zloty has the strongest potential to appreciate, back towards 4.30 against the euro, while the Czech koruna has practically none given the central bank's floor for EUR/CZK, Erste says. EUR/PLN is at 4.4059. In the case of Brexit, central banks in Croatia, Romania and Serbia would need to intervene to reduce currency volatility, Erste says. The Hungarian and Polish central banks would allow some currency depreciation--above 318 in EUR/HUF and 4.50 in EUR/PLN--and take action only in case of excessive market turbulence. title: Croatia  central bank  calls auction offering euros to banks
text:
ZAGREB, Sept 30 (Reuters) - Croatia's central bank called an auction on Wednesday to prop up the national kuna currency, which has eased against the euro in recent days as banks seek euros to implement the conversion of Swiss franc loans.

The kuna was quoted at 7.6680 per euro ahead of the intervention.

Croatia's banks need to adjust their foreign currency positions after the conversion of Swiss franc loans on their books into euros. The central bank said the country's currency reserves could fall by about a billion euros due to the conversion. (Reporting by Igor Ilic)

title: CEE MARKETS 2-  Currencies  and bonds ease ahead of talks on Greek debt
text:
* CEE currencies, bonds ease as euro group discusses Greek
bailout
    * Crown eases, central bank chief defends weak crown policy
    * Croatian central bank sells euro after kuna falls to
11-year low
    * Serbian buys euro to stem dinar surge ahead of bond
auctions

 (Recasts with fall in currencies, central bank interventions)
    By Sandor Peto and Jakub Iglewski
    BUDAPEST/WARSAW, Feb 20  (Reuters) - Central European
currencies and government bonds fell on Friday as concern grew
over Greece's future in the euro zone, the main export market of
the region's emerging economies.
    Later today, euro zone finance ministers will meet on
whether to extend a loan agreement that Greece urgently needs.
Its current bailout programme expires on Feb. 28. 
    "Greece is a No. 1 topic right now," one Warsaw-based
currency dealer said. "All that investors care about is to close
riskier positions before the weekend. Risk-off attitude is
dominating emerging markets today and the zloty is losing, too."
    The zloty slipped 0.4 percent against the euro by
1432 GMT. The forint, which earlier in the day traded
near a three-month high, shed 0.3 percent to 306.35. The leu
 eased 0.2 percent to 4.458. 
    Government bond yields rose, with Polish 10-year debt
trading at 2.33 percent, up 7 basis points and Hungary's
corresponding yield rising 1 basis point to 3.27 percent,
reversing an early drop.
    Analysts have said that the region's currencies and
relatively high-yielding government bonds could gain if Greece
reaches a deal on its debt.
    The Czech crown may be an exception. It decoupled
from its regional peers this week and got on a roller coaster
after Czech President Milos Zeman slammed the central bank's
"devaluation" policy. 
    The bank's governor, Miroslav Singer, reacted late on
Thursday, saying that the bank will not end its policy of
intervening if necessary to keep the crown weak before the
second half of 2016. 
    The crown eased half a percent against the euro to 27.531. 
    "In the next couple of days I see the crown in the range
27.400-700," one Prague-based dealer said. "The main factor is
Greece, of course. The market is quite nervous because of it." 
    The kuna bucked the regional trend, strengthening
by 0.2 percent against the euro to 7.713, after the Croatian
central bank sold 172.7 million euros to commercial banks. It
was the bank's second intervention this year to support the
kuna. 
    Companies in Croatia have been buying euros, while its
economy has contracted by about 13 percent in the past six
years. 
    Neighbouring Serbia's central bank, in contrast, sold euros
to stem a surge by the dinar, which it keeps in tight ranges.
The dinar still gained 0.7 percent to 120.14 per euro.
    The Serbian economy has also underperformed Central European
peers, but demand from foreign investors lifted the dinar before
next week's auctions of high-yielding 1-year and 3-year bonds,
dealers said.

title: CEE MARKETS 1-Assets in holding pattern as markets monitor Greek debt talks
text:
* Progress at Greek debt talks could lift CEE currencies,
bonds
    * Crown eases, central bank chief defends weak crown policy
    * Kuna hits 11-year low, central bank calls euro-selling
auction

    By Sandor Peto
    BUDAPEST, Feb 20  (Reuters) - Central European assets were
stuck in a holding pattern on Friday as investors awaited a
meeting of euro zone finance ministers to discuss Greece's
urgent need for more financial aid.
    If a deal can be reached, the region's currencies and
relatively high-yielding government bonds could climb. 
    Yields on debt in the region have risen in recent weeks from
near record lows on concerns over debt-laden Greece's future in
the euro zone.
    Hungary sold almost 50 percent more government bonds than
planned at its auctions on Thursday, however, with yields
falling in the secondary market. The yield on three-year paper
dropped a further six basis points on Friday to 2.18 percent.
    "As already witnessed yesterday, the upward pressure, mainly
on longer-dated LCY (local currency) yields in the region, eased
with hopes of a viable solution to the Greek debt crisis,"
Raiffeisen said in a note.
    Poland's zloty eased 0.2 percent against the euro
by 0931 GMT while Hungary's forint firmed 0.1 percent
to 305.06.
    One trader said recent data showing good economic growth had
buoyed the forint. Figures on Friday showed a 6.7 percent annual
rise in gross wages in December. 
    The Czech crown has been on a rollercoaster in the
last few days, decoupling from regional peers after Czech
President Milos Zeman slammed the central bank's "devaluation"
policy. 
    The bank's governor, Miroslav Singer, reacted late on
Thursday, saying that the bank will not end its policy of
intervening if necessary to keep the crown weak before the
second half of 2016. 
    The crown eased 0.2 percent against the euro to
27.435. 
    Raiffeisen said in its note that the crown could head back
towards 27.7, while Komercni Banka fixed income trader Dalimil
Vyskovsky said it could settle around 27.35.
    "We do not think another big drop would be a threat today,
however, the FX market will be a crucial guide for trading rates
in the next days, or weeks," he added.
    Croatia's kuna touched 11-year lows against the
euro at 7.733 in early trade. The central bank called an auction
to sell euros in its second intervention this year to prop up
the currency. 
    Companies in Croatia have been buying euros, while the
economy has contracted by about 13 percent in the past six
years.

title: CEE MARKETS 2-Polish bonds retreat; attention shifts to output data
text:
* Polish data leave rate cut outlook unchanged
    * CEE currencies, equities rebound, Fed still eyed
    * Serbian central bank intervenes to defend dinar
    * Floods hit Serbia, Croatia again

    By Sandor Peto
    BUDAPEST, Sept 16 (Reuters) - Polish government bonds
retreated on Tuesday after employment and corporate wage figures
for August suggested the country's central bank would not cut
rates any more than expected.
    The move also reflected a small rise in the yields of
long-dated euro zone government debt.
    Poland's 10-year benchmark yield rose to 3.07
percent from a morning low at 3.03 percent. Earlier, Poland
reported that wages rose 3.5 percent in August on an annual
basis and employment continued to grow, albeit at a slightly
slower pace of 0.7 percent.
    Analysts said industrial output figures due on Wednesday may
provide more clues about when the Polish central bank will cut
its main interest rate, now 2.5 percent, and by how much. The
consensus forecast is for 0.7 percent growth in output.
    If the output figure disappoints, "it may fuel expectations
that the overall (rate) cut will be bigger than we currently
expect (i.e. 25 basis pints in October and another 25 basis
points in November)," Erste said in a note.
    Economic slowdown, partly due to the effects of conflict in
Ukraine, have made the region's central banks, especially
Poland's, increasingly dovish in the past months.
    Concern that the Federal Reserve may signal at its meeting
on Wednesday that it will soon raise rates has weighed on
long-dated bonds in recent weeks. But expectations the European
Central Bank will begin a programme of asset purchases have
started to prop up bond prices, and yields are lower than they
were six weeks ago.   
    The average yield on the 3-month Treasury bills Hungary sold
at an auction stayed at record lows at 1.38 percent. Longer debt
yields even dropped by a few basis points in the secondary
market in low turnover.
    
    CONCERNS EASE
    Concern over Wednesday's Fed meeting and turmoil in Ukraine
had eased by afternoon trade, and the region's equities and
currencies mostly recovered from early declines.
    The loss of the stocks of Hungarian pharmaceuticals Richter
, which exports to Russia and Ukraine, narrowed to 0.36
percent from more than 1 percent. Budapest's main stock index
 gained 0.25 percent, although turnover remained low.
    Prague's main stock index was still down by 1.1
percent, dragged lower mainly by a 2 percent decline of
electricity producer CEZ PR>. CEZ fell on profit-taking;
its shares had risen more than 10 percent since early August.
    The shares of Slovenia's telecom operator, Telekom
, jumped by more than 6 percent to 137.5 euros after
incoming finance minister Dusan Mramor said late on Monday the
privatisation of Telekom will continue. Ljubljana's blue-chip
SBI index gained 1.9 pct. 
    The privatisation was put on hold earlier in September, 
awaiting approval of the sale by the new centre-left government
that is expected to be sworn in on Thursday. 
    The dinar rose a third of a percent against the
euro to 118.72, strongly outperforming regional peers, after
hitting two-year lows a week ago because of concern over a delay
in much-needed fiscal reforms in Serbia.
    Dealers said the Serbian central bank, which repeatedly
intervened this year to protect the currency, bought the dinar
in the market again in early trade. 
    Croatia's kuna eased 0.1 percent.
    One person died in Serbia and hundreds were evacuated due to
new floods in the Balkans. Severe floods in May killed dozens
and worsened Croatia's and Serbia's recession and fiscal
problems.

title: CEE MARKETS 3-Zloty leads  FX  bounce,  Croatia  cbank  intervenes
text:
* Romanian leu moves away from all-time low

* Stocks, bonds mixed as some Europe markets on holiday

* Hungary c.bank seen on hold while volatility persists

* Croatia c.bank intervenes to support kuna

(Adds Croatia details, comment)

By Jason Hovet and Sam Cage

PRAGUE/BUCHAREST, May 28 (Reuters) - Poland's zloty led central European currencies higher on Monday when investors dipped back into the region's riskier assets, though dealers said it was a short-term rebound and expectations of a rally looked misplaced.

Opinion polls on Saturday showed Greek conservatives regaining a lead that would allow the formation of a government that supports the country's international bailout, a commitment needed to keep the funds flowing.

With Europe's leaders now openly debating a possible exit of Greece from the euro zone, emerging EU assets have taken a beating this month due to the region's close banking, financing and export ties.

Markets are tipped to remain volatile until at least June 17, when Greeks vote again to choose a government that will largely determine if the country sticks with the euro.

By 1309 GMT the zloty, the region's most liquid currency, was bid 0.4 percent higher at 4.336 per euro.

The Romanian leu gained 0.3 percent to 4.467 after hitting a record low of 4.50 in late trade on Friday when the wealthiest Spanish region of Catalonia said it needed help with financing, showing the spread of the debt crisis.

The threat of central bank intervention to keep the currency away from lows was keeping the market on alert, dealers said.

"Overall it resembles more a relief rally in risky assets rather than a new trend," said one.

Stocks were mixed, with Bucharest a touch lower around a four-month low due to Romania's large exposure to Greece and Warsaw up 0.9 percent.

"Greek polls boosted sentiment, but we're not really seeing a significant increase in demand for riskier assets. It's more of a correction," said a Warsaw-based dealer

HUNGARY RATE CALL

Trading was muted with the U.S. and some major European centres closed for a holiday. In the debt market, Czech bond yields dipped, getting support from expectations of a rate cut in June. Polish yields were flat.

The Czech crown rose 0.3 percent and Hungary's forint, the most vulnerable in the region due to delays in getting an international credit line to help ease debt costs, rose 0.2 percent to in offshore trade with Budapest markets closed.

It has rebounded 2 percent since hitting a four-month low in the middle of last week.

The market turmoil is putting many central banks in a tight spot by impeding the reduction of interest rates that would help spur the economy.

Analysts expect the Hungarian central bank keep its growth-choking 7 percent base rate on hold on Tuesday, but they said the rate could be cut by 50 basis points by the end of the year if Hungary secures a loan from the International Monetary Fund and EU through talks that have been help up by policy disputes.

Croatia's central bank sold 266.4 million euros to commercial banks to prop up the kuna, which has come under mounting pressure in recent days as demand for euros from local banks has escalated, its fourth intervention this year.

The currency was bid 0.2 percent higher at 7.559 per euro, still weaker than the range of 7.50-7.55 in recent weeks under its managed float system.

"Despite this intervention... the kuna may remain exposed to depreciation pressures if demand for euros does not subside," a 


dealer at a major bank said.

title: Croatia cenbank calls auction to tame kuna gains
text:
ZAGREB, Oct 22 (Reuters) - The Croatian central bank called an auction on Thursday to buy euros from commercial banks in its second effort this month to ease appreciation pressures on the national kuna currency.

The kuna was quoted at 7.21 per euro before the auction, which will close at 0845 GMT.

The market had anticipated a possible intervention. The kuna has in recent days been exposed to appreciation pressures as banks have been adjusting hard-currency positions ahead of upcoming borrowing abroad by the government and some state agencies.

The central bank also intervened two weeks ago to tame upward pressures on the kuna by buying 154 million euros.

This is the central bank's fourth intervention on the foreign exchange market this year to counter kuna gains. It has also intervened twice to boost the kuna.

title: CEE MARKETS 4- FX  rebound on stocks, Polish cbank comments
text:
* FX mixed, mkt digests rate comments, decisions

* More weakening likely, say dealers

* Polish cbank does not rule out future fx intervention

* Croatia unveils anti-crisis package

(Adds new comments, fresh prices.)

By Sandor Peto and Dagmara Leszkowicz

BUDAPEST/WARSAW, Feb 26 (Reuters) - Central Europe's currencies inched up late on Thursday, bolstered by a cautious rise in global investors' appetite for risk and comments on intervention by the Polish central bank governor.

A rise by equities in Europe and a positive opening of stocks in the U.S. gave support to currencies across the emerging region, helping erase earlier losses for the Polish zloty <EURPLN=>.

The zloty also drew some strength, dealers said, from central bank Governor Slawomir Skrzypek, who said the bank might intervene in the currency market to support the zloty in certain conditions. [ID:nLQ831361]

But markets are sceptical on the chances of outright intervention by central banks at these levels, and currencies stayed in relatively tight ranges after recent sharp losses.

The zloty and the Romanian leu were flat against the euro at 1506 GMT at 4.692 and 4.286, respectively, while the Czech crown<EURCZK=> firmed 0.29 percent to 28.289. The Hungarian forint<EURHUF=> and the Croatian kuna<EURHRK=> both gained half a percent, to 299.63 and 7.35, after Croatia's government unveiled measures to counter the impacts of the global crisis.

Dealers and strategists said all would remain under pressure as the global crisis hits the region's export-heavy economies and concerns persist over their reliance on foreign financing.

"The trend (of weakening currencies) hasn't changed really so the recent strengthening could be a short-term correction," said Sylwester Brzeczkowski, dealer at ABN Amro in Warsaw.

If the currencies continue to slide, a key question is what governments and central banks in the region are ready to add to Monday's coordinated verbal intervention by central banks in the region.

The Polish government has moved the zloty by selling some of its EU fund inflows on the open market, and Czech Finance Minister Miroslav Kalousek said late on Wednesday that the government was considering all possible tools to help the undervalued crown.[ID:nLP635129]

DILEMMA

Poland's quarter-point interest rate cut on Wednesday highlighted the dilemma of banks which have been cutting rates to help the ailing economies but are worried lower interest rates -- which also cuts the premium paid for held assets -- could fuel more currency weakness.

"The central bank comments referring to further rate cuts weakened the Polish unit (on Wednesday), which counters Monday's coordinated regional central bank statement," Hungarian MKB Bank said in a note.

Hungary's central bank kept its rates on hold at its meeting early this week, pausing in its earlier monetary easing cycle due to concerns over the forint's weakness and its impact on the loan portfolio quality of domestic banks.

But the woes of the economy maintain pressure on the bank to cut interest rates further. Rate setter Julia Kiraly said there were downside risks to its forecasts for growth, which already predict a recession in 2009 and 2010 [ID:nLP831873].

The Polish central bank has lowered borrowing costs by a total of 200 basis points in the current easing cycle, bringing the key interest rate to 4.0 percent.

However Wednesday's cut was not as sharp as the previous ones, as the council pointed to recent zloty weakening and concerns over its volatility. [ID:nLP445602]

"While the sell-off has so far been indiscriminate and Emerging Europe assets are likely to remain under pressure for some time, past episodes show that market moves should eventually reflect country-specific conditions," said Neil Shearing, analyst at Capital Economics in a note.

Analysts view Poland and Czech Republic as being in better position to manage the global downturn than states like Romania or Hungary, which have ran higher current account deficits.

title: CEE MARKETS 3- FX  just down, stocks battered by risk flight
text:
(Updates throughout)

WARSAW/PRAGUE, Oct 24 (Reuters) - Romania's leu recovered a foothold in late trade on Friday after slumping as much as 4 percent earlier in the session due to an emerging market selloff that has battered central European currencies.

By 1510 GMT, the leu <EURRON=> had lost 1 percent on the day with markets across the region still weighed down by worries over Hungary and a wider global slowdown. The Bucharest stock exchange was temporarily shut after a more than 8 percent drop.

At 1417 GMT, Poland's zloty had nudged 0.1 percent down from Thursday's close to 3.84 per euro, well off session lows. The Czech crown <EURCZK=> lost 0.8 percent in illiquid trade.

A global sell-off swept through the region's stock markets, with Prague <.PX> down 11.8 percent to its lowest in four years, while Warsaw's blue-chip index <.WIG20> lost 4 percent and touched its lowest level since December 2003.

The Bucharest bourse was temporarily shut after a more than 8 percent drop.

Unwinding of positions has hit emerging markets this week as the global financial crisis prompted investors to pull money back to major western markets.

Worries over Hungary's external financing have sent the forint 15 percent lower since the start of October and forced its central bank into an emergency 3-percentage-point hike in interest rates on Wednesday. Hungarian markets were closed for a public holiday on Thursday and Friday.

The zloty has also shed 14.8 percent in October with heavy falls in the past couple days, leading Polish officials to step in and argue the move is not due to economic fundamentals.

Polish central bank Governor Slawomir Skrzypek stood by the bank's long-held hands-off policy on the currency on Friday, saying he did not foresee foreign exchange interventions for now [ID:nLO201754].

"The zloty fell just too much yesterday, and today we're seeing a technical bounce-back connected with the realization of profits," said Jakub Wiraszka, a trader at BRE Bank said.

With high local interest rates, Hungarian, Romanian and Polish households have more often opted for loans in foreign currencies, raising central Europe's credit exposure.

"Given these imbalances and vulnerabilities, the strong tightening in global credit conditions weighs heavily on local markets triggering a mechanical and natural adjustment of exchange rates," Societe Generale analyst wrote in a weekly currency report on Friday.

STANDING BY

Romania's leu <EURRON=> had gained strongly as banks scrambled to meet minimum reserve requirements this week.

The Romanian central bank has also intervened in some cases this month to prop up the currency, and analysts say this has helped lead to a jump in money market rates [ID:nLN111493].

In Serbia, the dinar <EURRSD=> fell to a five-month, but the central bank said it would not intervene [ID:nLO45368], while Croatia's kuna <EURHRK=> was steady, but analysts said pressure next week after recent losses could alert the central bank.

Polish bond yields dropped on Friday along with Czech yields, with dealers saying some market makers in Prague have started quoting after the Czech bond market seized up over the past month.

The Czech central bank has launched a repo facility that takes government bonds as collateral to boost liquidity, while Poland's central bank has already announced it would offer foreign currency swaps on a daily basis for banks.

title: UPDATE 1-Croat kuna eases after cenbank buys euros
text:
(Adds result of central bank intervention)   

ZAGREB, Jan 31 (Reuters) - Croatia's central bank said it had bought 189.1 million euros from banks at an average rate of 7.2458 kuna per euro at an auction on Thursday intended to ease upward pressure on the national currency.   

After the intervention, which the market largely expected, the kuna eased slightly to 7.2120/7.2180 per euro on the open interbank market from 7.2085/7.2185 in the morning -- its highest level since 2002.   

Dealers said the intervention should be enough to restrain the kuna this week.   

"But next week's (rate) movements depend on whether the central bank holds its weekly reverse repo auction on Wednesday," said a money market dealer from a local bank.   

The central has held only one reverse repo auction so far this year, saying it would hold the auctions when it deems necessary, instead of every week, to manage liquidity and the exchange rate.   

Thursday's intervention was the central bank's first this year to counter upward pressures on the kuna. Last year it intervened four times to cap the kuna, buying altogether 662 million euros from commercial banks.   

The kuna has firmed steadily after central bank governor Zeljko Rohatinski said last week the bank, prompted by inflationary pressures, would not allow the kuna to depreciate but controlled appreciation pressures were possible.   

The central bank, which keeps the kuna in a managed float, has never publicly said which floating band it targets, but analysts believe it is allowing the band to gradually move upwards.   

In the last few months, the kuna mostly traded at between 7.30 and 7.35 to the euro. By contrast, it floated at between 7.5 and 7.7. to the euro several years ago.

title: UPDATE 1-Croat cenbank  intervenes  to curb kuna strength
text:
(Adds analyst quotes, details)  

ZAGREB, June 2 (Reuters) - Croatia's central bank staged its heaviest intervention this year on the foreign exchange market on Friday to curb the pressures on the local kuna currency to appreciate.  

The bank said it had bought 104.3 million euros from banks at an average rate of 7.258188 kuna per euro at an auction. Its dollar purchases were greater than on any of the five occasions earlier this year when it stepped into the market.  

The kuna<EURHRK=> inched down to 7.2528/7.2628 to the euro from a five-year high of 7.2490/7.2570, where it had stood before the intervention, which did not surprise the market despite its unusual timing.  

"The timing of the intervention, Friday afternoon, may be indicative as the central bank normally did not use to intervene at this time. It may show its determination to keep the kuna at the current level," a foreign exchange dealer at a major local bank said.  

The central bank has intensified interventions on the local foreign exchange market in recent weeks amid steady appreciation pressures on the kuna. However, the interventions have had only a short-term effect.  

"Appreciation pressures are strong and steady as there is strong credit activity based on funds from abroad, besides foreign investments and rising tourist income," the dealer said.  

This year the central bank has bought altogether 407.5 million euros from commercial banks in its six interventions to curb the kuna.  

The previous intervention took place on May 15 when the central bank bought 69.6 million euros at an average rate of 7.275064 kuna per euro.  

Central bank governor Zeljko Rohatinski said last month the bank would react strongly if faced with considerable appreciation pressures, but did not elaborate what measures it could take on top of interventions on the local foreign exchange market.  

Analysts expect the kuna to firm further as the tourist summer season gets into full swing and inflow of euros, as well as demand for the kuna, intensifies.  

They say steady appreciation pressures are almost certain as the country nears EU membership, adding that the kuna might firm to as much as 7.10 per -euro or even beyond in the coming years.  

Croatia opened talks on EU membership with Brussels last October.

text:

ZAGREB, Feb 16 (Reuters) - Croatia's central bank bought 83.1 million euros from banks at its auction on Thursday to cap the kuna gains, but the national currency shrugged it off to firm to new highs in interbank trading.  

The central bank bought the euros at an average rate of 7.310213 kuna per euro in its second intervention in as many weeks, which the market largely expected.  

The kuna <EURHRK=>, which eased slightly after the auction, soon rebounded to a fresh six-month high of 7.29/7.30 per euro.  

"Another failed attempt by the central bank to rein in the kuna. There is obviously a huge amount of euros on the market. We think the kuna will firm on and expect another intervention soon," said a foreign exchange dealer at a local bank.  

The central bank previously intervened to cap the kuna on Feb. 2, when it was quoted at 7.33/7.34.  

The kuna has been trading at between 7.35 and 7.42 versus the euro since Croatia opened European Union entry talks last October. But it appreciated steadily in recent days amid increased demand, as investors collected funds for a new local bond issue due on Friday.

title: Croat kuna seen firming as EU entry nears-analysts
text:
ZAGREB, Feb 1 (Reuters) - Croatia's kuna currency is likely to appreciate steadily as the former Yugoslav republic moves towards European Union membership, analysts said on Wednesday.  

The central bank keeps the kuna in a managed float regime and until last year it had strengthened in the summer months, amid strong inflow of hard currency from tourism, before gradually easing during the winter season.  

A year ago it traded around 7.51/7.52 per euro, but has held at stronger levels since Zagreb opened EU entry talks last October. On Wednesday morning it traded at 7.34/7.35 on the open interbank market.  

"Inflows of foreign capital as we approach the EU support a strong kuna," said Mladen Smiljanic of Zagrebacka Banka.  

"The central bank will certainly act to keep appreciation under control," Smiljanic said, but he added that it was not unimaginable to see the kuna firming towards 7.10 per euro in the coming years.  

The central bank never publicised its targeted exchange rate band, but it was widely thought that it tolerated a five percent floating band ranging from 7.30 in the summer to 7.70 in the winter season.  

In the last few months, the central bank intervened each time when the kuna was threatening to pierce the 7.35 support level, but this week it let it slip.  

"The banks mostly adhered to that level as they deemed the intervention imminent if they should breach it. The kuna could firm towards 7.25 per one euro this summer, but a lot depends on how the central bank will react," said Hrvoje Dolenec, an analyst at Raiffeisenbank.  

ROOM FOR GAINS  

Lars Christensen of Danske Bank said current appreciation pressures reflected positive sentiment on the international markets, as investors expect Croatia to join the EU before the end of the decade.  

"There is substantial room for kuna gains against the euro. If there were a free float, the kuna would be considerably stronger. The central bank will not allow it, but gradual easing of the (intervention) policy is possible," he said.  

Croatian exporters have often complained that too strong a kuna was hampering their business and voiced dissatisfaction with the central bank's exchange rate policy.  

But a central bank source recently told Reuters that it had acted to stop the currency climbing much faster and further.  

"Through our interventions on the market, we prevent the kuna from appreciating more than is actually the case," the source said.  

Last year the central bank bought 570.8 million euros ($692.2 million) from commercial banks in nine interventions to cap the kuna.

title: Emerging  FX -High-yielders retreat on dollar revival.
text:
LONDON, Dec 8 (Reuters) - A recovery in the dollar caused high-yield emerging market currencies to retreat from their highs on Wednesday, with falling gold prices and the risk of a rate cut adding to downward pressure on the South African rand. The dollar rallied one percent off Tuesday's record lows against the euro as investors bought back the U.S. currency in the run-up to the year's end and watched the impact of dollar weakness on other economies.  

The South African rand was also caught up in a broader commodity currency retreat, with the Canadian and Australian dollars falling sharply after both central banks kept interest rates on hold.  

"The rand move is very much a reflection of the broad dollar correction and also the sharp gold correction, which has a big impact on the rand," said Tania Kotsos, emerging markets currency strategist at Royal Bank of Canada.  

Bullion prices fell over $7.00 on Wednesday to around $445 per ounce . South Africa is the world's largest gold producer.  

By 1046 GMT, the rand was down around 1.5 percent against the dollar at 5.85 .  

Concern that the central bank was starting to become more wary of rand strength also weighed on the currency after central bank governor Tito Mboweni said he preferred a competitive exchange rate.  

Most analysts polled by Reuters last week expected the central bank to keep key interest rates steady at 7.5 percent at its monetary policy decision on Thursday.  

However, the rand's charge to six-year highs against the dollar this month may have raised the chances of a cut, thanks to the dampening effect it has on inflation.  

Kotsos said the rand pullback was likely to prove temporary: "This is not trend reversal but more an opportunity to re-enter short dollar positions.  

"Any correction is likely to see exporters flood in to buy rand." Exporters are natural rand buyers to convert the proceeds of overseas earnings.  

Kotsos said key resistance in dollar/rand was at 5.89/5.90 per dollar, with another layer seen at 5.95/5.96.  

ZLOTY PEGGED BACK  

The Polish zloty also dropped back in line with the broadly soft emerging market tone, with Finance Minister Miroslaw Gronicki casting some doubt on how long the rally could continue.  

"We have a floating exchange rate. Today the zloty is strengthening, in 3-4 months the situation may be reversed," he said. Deutsche Bank strategist Caio Natividade said: "Gronicki's statements are interesting in that he seems to be shifting emphasis towards rate cut environment.  

"In fact, after recent comments from the central bank, that is already in the process of being priced into the money markets."  

He added that didn't change the bank's bullish view on the zloty.  

"On a real effective basis versus the euro it may be around fair value, but when you consider other measures such as unit labour costs and the structural appreciation of other currencies in the region it is still undervalued."   


The zloty traded at 4.2040 to the euro  from 4.1778 late on Tuesday and
at 3.1551 to the dollar        from 3.1116.
  

This week has seen a string of countries intervene to curb currency strength and Croatia was the latest on Wednesday.  

The Croatian central bank called a currency tender on Wednesday, its first since mid-September, offering to buy euros from banks to halt the kuna's gains.  

The kuna jumped to 7.46/7.47 per euro , its highest since late October, prior to the tender, following a large euro sell order from a domestic bank on Tuesday. The kuna later eased back to trade at 7.4950/7.5050.

LONDON, July 6 (Reuters) - The lira traded around two-month highs versus the dollar on Tuesday amid optimism about Turkey's economic outlook, while the Croatian kuna was pushed down against the euro by central bank intervention.  

Last week's data releases which included first quarter annual economic growth at 12.4 percent and benign inflation gave a broad boost to Turkish markets.  

Investor appetite for higher-yielding currencies has also helped the lira since the Federal Reserve's U.S. interest rate hike last week and its pledge for "measured" policy steps in the future.  

"The global dynamic is generally more friendly towards high yielders now and this is helping the likes of the Turkish lira," said Callum Henderson, head of emerging market foreign exchange and fixed income research at Bank of America in London.  

"The domestic picture in Turkey is also supportive."  

"We don't expect rampant appreciation but a slow grind lower (in dollar versus lira)," he said.  

At 1000 GMT the Turkish lira traded at1.434 million per dollar , up some half a percent on the day and near the 1.43 million area where it set a two-month high earlier in the day.  

Headline inflation figures on Saturday showed Turkey's year-end IMF-backed targets were within reach. Consumer prices fell a monthly 0.13 percent, while wholesale prices were down 1.05 percent.  

Analysts have said that the price data could encourage Turkey's central bank to cut interest rates within the next month but it is expected to remain cautious in the near term. Official interest rates are at 22 and 27 percent, far above the Fed's 1.25 percent rate.  

May industrial production data are due out on Thursday and expected to show annual growth of 16.5 percent.  

KUNA INTERVENTION

title: Croatia  c.bank to  intervene  to support kuna if necessary.
text:
ZAGREB, Jan 28 (Reuters) - The Croatian central bank said on Tuesday it was closely watching the kuna's steady depreciation this month and would not hesitate to intervene to maintain its stability. 

 The kuna , which has fallen to an 11-month low, was quoted at 7.56/7.57 against the euro on the interbank market on Tuesday. Its depreciation has accelerated since January 15 when it stood at 7.47/48 per euro. 

 The central bank last intervened on January 7 when it sold 74.6 million euros to banks at a fixed 7.52 kuna. 

 Deputy central bank governor Boris Vujcic told Reuters the depreciation was seasonal and typical for the start of the year. 

 "We always have depreciation at this time of the year so this is nothing out of the ordinary framework of the exchange rate movements," he said. 

 Demand for hard currency rises substantially in January, mostly because of foreign debt servicing, both corporate and government. 

 "The central bank will be watching the rate to assess if and when to intervene. We have all the instruments to control the exchange rate at our disposal and we shall continue to use them when needed," Vujcic added. 

 Some observers ascribed the depreciation - on top of strong hard currency demand by corporate clients - to commercial banks' efforts to build a long hard currency position before a new central bank rule on asset/liability ratios takes effect in February. 

 The ratio will now be monitored every day instead of the previous practice of monitoring it only once a month. Some banks have met the ratio by taking out short-term loans abroad and then repaying them. 

 Vujcic said it was too early to assess the effects of the new measure. "We will need to follow the trends in the next few months to evaluate their effect". 

 A dealer said that after banks have built up larger hard currency positions to meet the new rule "the effect on the exchange rate will diminish." 

 The central bank, which has maintained monetary stability since slashing hyperinflation in 1993, has a managed float regime, whereby it keeps the kuna within a desirable band to the euro, intervening on the foreign exchange market when necessary. 

 "We don't announce the band and don't have a targeted band. We assess the exchange rate, as well as macro and micro economic indicators, at every moment to decide when an intervention is necessary," Vujcic said.

title: INTERVIEW-Croatian c.bank sees no need to fix kuna.
text:
ZAGREB, May 21 (Reuters) - The Croatian central bank sees no need to change the course of its policy or fix the kuna, although its rally threatens to undermine the impending tourist season, governor Zeljko Rohatinski said on Monday. 

 "Fixing the kuna would make no sense. It would be a move directed against the market. It would not work," Rohatinski told Reuters in an interview. 

 The current exchange rate is a managed float, determined by the market, where the central bank intervenes to iron out oscillations that are too strong or bear on other developments. 

 The kuna fluctuates seasonally, appreciating on the inflow of hard currency from privatisation, state borrowings abroad and earnings from the flagship tourist trade during the summer. 

 It has hit a three-year peak of 7.3 to the euro this week, after firming more and earlier than usual on proceeds from two foreign debt issues in March. 

 A switch in Croatian banks' investment, due to a global fall of interest rates, from foreign deposits into credits to local borrowers has also contributed. Year-to-April money supply rose some 36 percent and bank credits to the corporate and private borrowers 17 percent. 

 "These are positive and welcome developments," Rohatinski said, adding they were partly a result of the central bank's gradual cuts in the banks' mandatory reserves since last year. 

 "So there is no need or possibility to change the exchange rate regime with a satisfactory outcome, while maintaining the same monetary policy course." 

 NO BOWING TO PRESSURE 

 Last week, businessmen and tourism officials complained against the kuna strength and called on the central bank to intervene ahead of the summer to help Croatia gain some competitive advantage over other regional destinations. 

 "Such positions of these and other export-oriented companies are understandable and legitimate," Rohatinski said. 

 "But there is a difference between hotel competitiveness, as their prices are for the most part agreed in advance and expressed in foreign currencies anyway, and spending on other services outside hotels which may indeed be adversely affected. 

 "However, the foreign exchange policy and exchange rate movements cannot be determined from the aspect of just one branch of the economy or one region," he added. 

 There have also been suggestions from banking circles to introduce the euro as a new currency, but the governor also ruled these out as "unilateral moves that would not help Croatia's bid to join the European Union". 

 Instead, the central bank board last week approved a further cut in the reserve ratio for banks to 22 percent from July to increase kuna liquidity. 

 At the same time it expanded the reserve base by including additional foreign exchange funds to also reduce their supply. 

 But further action is to some extent limited by the fact that two thirds of the broadest monetary aggregate, the M4, are euro funds. They represent a high 80 percent of all deposits. 

 "Such conditions...are practically tying our hands and limiting further interventions," Rohatinski said. 

 The bank now planned to intervene through minor foreign currency purchases to iron out the exchange rate fluctuations without risking the creation of inflationary pressure by pumping in too much money. 

 "It would be a vicious circle of the kind we have seen in the past," Rohatinski said. "It would not do to prevent the kuna appreciation by issuing so much money to cause inflation, and end up 'sinking the drowning man'."

title: Croatia  c.bank  intervenes  with swap  intervention .
text:
ZAGREB, June 4 (Reuters) - Croatia's central bank said it intervened in the foreign exchange market on Thursday with a swap intervention, selling 18.7 million German marks to commercial banks. 

 The marks were sold at a rate of 3.6435 kuna and will be bought back on July 24 at a forward rate, which dealers said would be 3.6980 kuna. 

 The central bank sold 57.15 million German marks at an average rate of 3.6257 kuna last Thursday in an outright sale.

title: Croatia c.bank sells marks, dlrs in  forex  market.
text:
ZAGREB, May 28 (Reuters) - Croatia's central bank said it intervened in the foreign exchange market on Thursday by selling marks and dollars to commercial banks. 

 It sold 57.15 million marks at an average rate of 3.6257 kuna and $0.5 million at 6.4580 kuna each, the bank said. 

 "Banks were buying to improve their (currency) positions," said one dealer at a large bank. 

 The bank last sold marks at 3.6092 and dollars at 6.4600 on May 19.

title: Croatian c.bank says buys hard  currency  from banks.
text:
ZAGREB, May 27 (Reuter) - Croatia's central bank said on Tuesday it had intervened on the foreign exchange market by buying hard currency from the banking sector. 

 The bank bought 22 million German marks at an average rate of 3.5643 kuna and $2.0 million at an average 6.0227 kuna per dollar, it said in a news release. 

 The central bank will issue kuna to commercial banks in two days and boost money supply for some 90 million kuna. 

 Due to stronger tourism inflows during the summer, it usually buys more foreign currency from banks and exchange offices in part also to prevent a stronger nominal appreciation of the kuna exchange rate. 

 The kuna was quoted at 6.0185 to the dollar and 3.5716 to the mark before today's intervention. -- Kolumbina Bencevic, Zagreb Newsroom, 385-1-4557075

title: Croatia 's  central bank intervenes  in  forex  market.
text:
ZAGREB, May 20 (Reuter) - Croatia's central bank said on Tuesday it had intervened in the foreign exchange market by buying and selling German marks. 

 "We had two goals: to prevent (the kuna) exchange rate appreciation due to stronger currency inflow and to help liquidity of the money market," a bank official told Reuters. 

 The bank bought 11.1 million marks at an average rate of 3.5700 kuna, it said in a statement faxed to Reuters. 

 This will result in an injection of just under 40 million kuna into the hard-pressed banking sector in two days. But there was no immediate reaction from the money market. 

 The official said this type of intervention would be more frequent during the summer as more hard currency from tourism createS an increased demand for kuna by banks and exchange offices, boosting upward pressure on the kuna rate. 

 The bank today also sold two million marks at the same average rate of 3.5700 kuna per mark, it said. 

 -- Kolumbina Bencevic, Zagreb Newsroom, 385-1-4557075

title: Croatia's c. bank sells marks, kuna firms.
text:
ZAGREB, Feb 26 (Reuter) - Croatia's central bank said it intervened on the foreign exchange market on Wednesday by selling commercial banks 36.6 million German marks at an average rate of 3.5819 kuna. 

 The bank also bought from the banking sector 3.0 million marks at an average 3.5681 kuna to the mark, it said in a press release. 

 In a move unrelated to its operations, the kuna midrate for Thursday's dealings against the dollar firmed to 5.9601 from 5.9890. But the kuna-mark rate was little affected, firming very marginally to 3.5702 from 3.5710. 

 The midrates are calculated as a weighted average of commercial banks' sell rates and therefore immune to their large purchases. 

 -- Zagreb Newsroom, 385-1-4557075

title: Croatia c.bank sells HRK128 mln bills, rates steady.
text:
ZAGREB, Jan 29 (Reuter) - Croatia's central bank auctioned 128 million kuna ($21.9 million) worth of 35- and 91-day liquidity bills at steady rates on Wednesday. 

 Because banks that have access to bill sales had high liquidity, volume rose from only 22.5 million issued last week. 

 Banks can use central bank paper as collateral for Lombard loans, granted at 11 percent. 

 The National Bank of Croatia also intervenes in the money market by occasionally buying or selling kuna for foreign exchange. 

 -- Kolumbina Bencevic, Zagreb Newsroom, 385-1-4557075

title: Croatian lending rate flat at 27.6 percent.
text:
ZAGREB, May 23 (Reuter) - The Croatian average lending rate was flat at 27.6 percent in slow trade because of slack demand for kuna funds on the Zagreb Money Market. 

 Total settlements rose slightly to 23.6 million kuna, leaving a surplus of more than 30 million for the third day in a row. 

 Call money, mostly made up of inter-bank placements at 28 percent, eased 10 basis points to 27.9 percent. The five-10 day rate rose to 27.4 from 27 percent. 

 Overnight supply met demand for 258 million kuna on Thursday without central bank intervention. 

 The National Bank of Croatia said it stayed out of the foreign exchange market today as well. Its kuna midrate eased to 5.571 against the dollar while firming to 6.174 to the mark. -- Kolumbina Bencevic, Zagreb Newsroom, 385-1-4557075

title: Croatian kuna peaks vs mark after c.bank purchase.
text:
ZAGREB, May 17 (Reuter) - The Croatian kuna hit this year's record high of 3.6306 against the German mark on Thursday after the central bank bought foreign exchange at a lower than market rate. 

 On Wednesday, the National Bank of Croatia intervened to ease the pressure on liquidity by purchasing from the banking sector 23.5 million marks at an average rate of 3.6109 kuna and $2.4 million at 5.4992 kuna to the dollar. 

 As a result, the kuna jumped from 3.6437 to the mark, , according to the central bank's midrate -- a weighted average of commercial banks' sell rates. 

 And the kuna firmed to 5.5563 to the dollar today, rising from 5.5854. 

 It was the third large purchase this year after repeated pleas by banks, which have been swimming in hard currency after a stronger seasonal inflow during the Easter holidays. 

 -- Kolumbina Bencevic, Zagreb Newsroom, 385-1-4557075

title: Better supply pushes Croatian kuna rate down.
text:
ZAGREB, April 2 (Reuter) - Better supply of kuna funds at lower rates pushed down the Croatian average lending rate on Tuesday to 28.6 percent from 29.0 percent in more active trade. 

 The Zagreb Money Market reported supply rising to 43.6 million kuna from 30.2 million, against 90 million demand. 

 It said 15 million kuna were placements by the state investment bank HBOR at 26 and 27 percent. The interbank lending rate was flat at 30 percent. 

 Most rates declined with only the rate for loans under five days edging up to 30 from 29.4 percent on March 29. 

 Call money, which accounted for most of the money market activities, was down to 29.2 from 29.9 percent. 

 The 31-366 day rate fell to 26 from 30 percent on March 27 and the five-10 day rate eased 20 basis points to 29.0 percent. 

 Overnight settlements to eight banks with shortfalls totalled 213.5 million kuna last night. 

 The overnight rate has been fixed at 19 percent, in line with the central bank intervention rate. 

 The National Bank of Croatia stayed out of the foreign exchange market today. It calculated the kuna midrate at 5.4701 to the dollar and at 3.6938 to the German mark. -- Kolumbina Bencevic, Zagreb Newsroom, 385-1-4557075

title: Croatian overnight rate flat at 29.4 pct.
text:
ZAGREB, March 28 (Reuter) - The Croatian overnight rate, a weighted average of interbank rates, was flat at 29.4 percent on Thursday despite a firming in the main lending rates as the supply of kuna funds on the local money market halved. 

 The five-10 day and call money rates edged up 10 basis points to 30 percent. 

 On a smaller volume, the rate for loans under five days rose a whole percentage point to 30 percent from March 26. 

 Total settelments shrank slightly to 19.9 from 21.7 million kuna against 40 million supply. The Zagreb Money Market reported demand rising to 25 from 23 millio kuna. 

 Overnight loans to six banks with shortfalls totalled 206.4 million kuna last night without central bank intervention. 

 The National Bank of Croatia said no commercial banks bid for foreign exchange at its auction without limit or a set exchange rate. It calculated the kuna midrate at 5.4867 to the dollar and at 3.6990 to the German mark. -- Kolumbina Bencevic, Zagreb Newsroom, 385-1-4557075

title: Croatian overnight, main lending rate eases.
text:
ZAGREB, March 8 (Reuter) - The overnight rate eased to 29.4 percent on Friday from 29.5 in line with the decline in the main kuna lending rates on the local money market. 

 The rate for five-10 day loans, which took up most of the day's interbank trading, dropped 20 basis points to 29.3 percent from yesterday. 

 The 31-366 day rates dropped to 29.0 percent from Monday 30.0. 

 The 15-30 day rates were unchanged at 29.9 percent and call money remained flat at 30.0 percent. 

 The Zagreb Money market reported demand at 58 million kuna, overstripping supply by almost 20 million. 

 Overnight loans, totalling 153.6 million kuna last night, left a shortfall of 113 million at one commercial bank which was covered by a central bank intervention loan. 

 The National Bank of Croatia stayed out of the foreign exchange market today. It calculated the kuna midrate at 5.4846 to the dollar and 3.6968 to the German mark. -- Zoran Radosavljevic, Zagreb Newsroom, 385-41-4550893

title: Croatian overnight rate eases to 29.3 pct.
text:
ZAGREB, March 6 (Reuter) - The Croatian overnight rate, a weighted average of the kuna interbank rates, eased to 29.3 percent on Wednesday from 29.5 percent in line with a slight decline in some of the main rates. 

 Call money eased 10 basis points to 30 percent. 

 The rates for five-10 loans, which accounted for most of the day's lending, was flat at 29.2 percent. The 15-30 day loans were made at 29 percent, also unchanged from yesterday. 

 The Zagreb Money Market reported total settlements rising very slightly to 21 million kuna, against 31 million demand. 

 Overnight supply, totalling 160.6 million kuna last night, left 62 million kuna shortfalls at commercial banks. 

 The National Bank of Croatia stepped in with intervention funds to two banks, while another one used an 11 million kuna Lombard loan for liquidity. 

 The central bank stayed out of the foreign exchange market today. It calculated the kuna midrate at 5.442 to the dollar and at 3.6985 to the German mark. -- Kolumbina Bencevic, Zagreb Newsroom, 385-1-4557075

title: Croatian overnight rate falls to 30.5 vs 31.6 pct.
text:
ZAGREB, Feb 22 (Reuter) - The Croatian overnight rate fell to 30.5 percent on Thursday from 31.6 percent in line with a decline in the main kuna interbank rates on which it is based. 

 Call money fell to 30.1 from 32.5 percent. The rate for five-10 day loans was down 30 basis points to 30.0 percent. 

 But the 15-30 day rate rose to 30 from 29.2 percent on February 16. 

 Total settlements through the Zagreb Money Market shrank to 19 million kuna from 30.9 million yesterday. Demand was reported unchanged at 50 million kuna. 

 Last night, with the help of 206.4 million kuna overnight funds all seven commercial banks with shortfalls managed to square their positions without central bank intervention. 

 The National Bank of Croatia held no foreign exchange auction today as the kuna held stable against the main hard currencies. It calculated the kuna medium rate at 5.3725 to the dollar and at 3.6970 to the German mark. -- Kolumbina Bencevic, Zagreb Newsroom, 385-1-4557075

title: Croatian overnight rate rises to 30.2 vs 29.9 pct.
text:
ZAGREB, Feb 19 (Reuter) - The Croatian overnight rate rose to 30.2 percent on Monday from 29.9 percent amid upward corrections in some of the interbank rates on which it is based, despite weaker demand. 

 Call money rose 20 basis points to 31.9 percent. But the five-10 day rate was down to 29.1 percent from 30. 

 The Zagreb Money Market reported settlements at 58.3 million kuna, of which 22.3 million were prolonged loans. Demand shrank to 67 from 85 million kuna last Friday. 

 Overnight supply, totalling 429 million kuna at the weekend, was outstripped by demand. The National Bank of Croatia granted an additional 177.6 million kuna intervention funds to help the banks square their positions. 

 The central bank said it held no foreign exchange auction today. It calculated the kuna medium rate at 5.4333 to the dollar and at 3.7019 to the mark. -- Kolumbina Bencevic, Zagreb Newsroom, 385-1-4557075

title: Croatian overnight rate eases to 29.5 pct.
text:

 The rate for 31-366 day loans jumped to 29.5 from 29.0 percent on January 23. The five-10 day rate rose to 29.3 from Friday's 29.0 percent. 

 Overnight borrowing totalled 315.3 million kuna on Saturday and all banks managed to square their positions without central bank intervention. 

 The National Bank of Croatia said no commercial banks bid for foreign exchange at its open-limit auction today.

title: Better supply keeps Croatia overnight rate stable.
text:
ZAGREB, Jan 16 (Reuters) - Better supply of kuna funds kept the overnight interest rate stable at 29.4 percent despite a slight rise in some interbank rates on which it is based. 

 The rate for 31-366 day loans jumped to 30 from 27.8 percent on January 8. Call money rose to 30 from 29.7 percent. 

 Five-10 day rate was unchanged at 29.0 percent. 

 Yesterday, overnight loans shrank to 187.8 from 267.8 million kuna at the weekend, leaving a surplus of 60 million. 

 One bank used an intervention loan from the central bank to square its position. The National Bank of Croatia grants intervention loaans at 19 percent. 

 The bank said its foreign exchange auction, aimed at mopping up excess liquidity, fell through for the second day in a row because of an absence of bidders. It sets no targeted exchange rate or limit on the amount on offer. 

 Today, the central bank quoted the kuna at 5.3554 to the dollar and at 3.7054 to the German mark. -- Kolumbina Bencevic, Zagreb Newsroom, 385-1-4557075

title: Croatia interbank rate jumps to 25.4 from 24.6 pct.
text:
ZAGREB, Dec 14 (Reuter) - The Croatian interbank rate jumped to 25.4 from 24.6 percent, pushed by an overwhelming demand for kuna funds on the money market. 

 The Zagreb Money Market reported a demand for 125 million kuna against only 14.4 million kuna supply, some of which was settled at a rate of 30 percent. 

 Call money rose to 28.4 from 26 percent on Wednesday and five-10 day rate went up to 24.2 percent from 23.9. 

 The rate for 31-366 day loans moved down to 24.3 from 26 percent on December 1. 

 Overnight loans, made at the average daily lending rate, totalled 87.1 million kuna, leaving a shortage of 240.6 million kuna at two commercial banks. 

 This was partly covered by a central bank intervention loan to one bank, while the other had to use mandatory reserve to square its position. 

 The National Bank of Croatia grants intervention loans to banks three times a month for a maximum of two days. 

 It said it had no foreign exchange operations on the market today. The bank calculated its weighted exchange rate for the kuna at 5.3691 to the dollar and 3.7172 to the German mark. 

 -- Kolumbina Bencevic, Zagreb Newsroom, 385-1-4557075

title: Croatia  central bank  raises reserve requirement.
text:
ZAGREB, May 9 (Reuter) - Croatia's central bank has set a new higher reserve requirement for banks, to regulate money flows, said Adolf Matejka, director for central bank operations at the National Bank of Croatia. 

 "The reserve ratio has been raised to 29.8 percent from 28.3 PErcent currently," he said 

 In November, the bank introduced a single 28.30 percent reserve ratio for banks and a new 7.50 percent ratio for other savings institutions. The former replaced 27.50 percent applied previously on sight deposits and deposits of up to three months, and 16 percent on deposits exceeding three months. 

 Matejka told Reuters the latest raise in the ratio had been approved to cut down excessive money supply growth and create more space for intervention in the foreign exchange markets in the coming period. 

Croatia gets a large inflow of foreign currency during summer tourist season, increasing demand for domestic currency at commercial banks and money changers. 

 To compensate for the higher reserve requirement, the central bank is to pay 5.50 percent interest on obligatory reserve instead of 5.15 it has paid to commercial banks so far. -- Kolumbina Bencevic, Zagreb Newsroom, 385-1-457075
